arguments.heading: Argument session of April 27, 2026
paragraphs: Chief Justice Roberts opened the session and recognized Monsanto's counsel. Three lawyers argued: Clement for Monsanto, Harris for the United States supporting Monsanto, and Keller for the Missouri side. [official source, official source]

Monsanto asked the Court to hold that FIFRA bars a state failure-to-warn claim demanding a cancer warning EPA did not require. It stressed that registrants cannot add warnings unilaterally; EPA approval is required. [official source, official source]
The United States asked the Court to find express and impossibility preemption. It cited federal rules requiring adherence to the EPA-approved label and governing hazard statements.
The Missouri side asked the Court to allow the suit. Keller argued registration is no misbranding defense and misbranding is not limited to label-registration matching.

Justices tested assumptions. One asked whether preemption stems from statute, regulations, or labeling requirements. Kavanaugh asked whether deviating from the approved label violates federal law, and whether differing state outcomes conflict with uniformity. [official source, official source, official source]

Kagan asked what uniformity the the opposing side's approach achieves under FIFRA's uniformity clause. Roberts asked Monsanto to distinguish Riegel. Alito asked whether Loper Bright addresses preemption or only separation of powers. [official source, official source, official source]

Answers followed. Monsanto said a registered product sold with the approved label is not misbranded. The United States said EPA requires data for changes, no unilateral change exists, and impossibility preemption applies. Keller distinguished Riegel on statutory grounds and preserved parallel claims. [official source, official source, official source]
No reargument occurred in this session, so nothing was revisited or changed by a later session. The approved record supports no further positions or facts beyond those described here.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: Monsanto sells a weed killer. Its label passed federal approval. A Missouri lawsuit still blamed it for cancer and demanded a stronger warning. The question is whether federal pesticide law blocks that state suit.
Federal pesticide law is called FIFRA. It lets the EPA approve product labels. Monsanto says once EPA approves a label, states cannot demand different warnings. [official source, official source]

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The case reached the Supreme Court as number 24-1068. The Court heard argument on April 27, 2026, in Washington. Chief Justice Roberts opened the session and called on Monsanto's lawyer first. [official source, official source, official source]
Three lawyers argued. Paul Clement argued for Monsanto. Sarah Harris argued for the United States, backing Monsanto. Ashley Keller argued for the Missouri side.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Monsanto asks the Court to rule that state law cannot force a cancer warning the EPA did not require. It says federal law preempts, meaning overrides, the state claim.
Monsanto also says a company cannot add warnings alone. EPA approval is needed first. So a state cannot demand a change the company cannot legally make by itself.
The United States agrees with Monsanto. It says Missouri demands a warning while federal rules require sticking to the EPA-approved label. Those two demands cannot both be obeyed.

The Missouri side asks the Court to let the lawsuit proceed. Its lawyer argues EPA registration is no shield against misbranding claims. Misbranding, he says, is not only about matching the registration paperwork.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Monsanto's core position: a product registered with EPA and sold with the approved label is not misbranded. That answers the state's accusation directly.

The United States adds that EPA requires data before label changes happen. No company can unilaterally rewrite warnings. When state law forces a change, prior cases called impossibility preemption apply.
The Missouri side answers the other way. Its lawyer says federal approval does not excuse misbranding, and misbranding reaches more than label-to-registration mismatches.
He also distinguished an earlier drug case called Riegel. He said this law has no matching provision, no statutory label lock, and preserves parallel claims.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: One justice asked where the preemption comes from: the statute, regulations, or the labeling rule itself. That probes the foundation of Monsanto's argument.
Justice Kavanaugh asked whether deviating from the EPA-approved label would itself violate federal law. That tests whether the Missouri warning demand is even possible.
Justice Kavanaugh also pressed the Missouri side. He said differing state liability outcomes clash with national uniformity.
Justice Kagan asked what uniformity the Missouri approach achieves under FIFRA's uniformity clause. That question cuts the other way.

Chief Justice Roberts asked Monsanto's lawyer to distinguish the Riegel case. Justice Alito asked whether Loper Bright concerns preemption or only separation of powers. [official source, official source]

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: The ruling could shape many pesticide lawsuits. If Monsanto wins, EPA-approved labels would shield companies from state warning claims. If the Missouri side wins, juries in different states could reach different results. [official source, official source]
The justices' questions show the tension. Uniformity favors one national rule. But FIFRA's own text and preserved state claims cut toward allowing some lawsuits. [official source, official source]

sections.heading: What happens next
paragraphs: The Court has heard argument but has not decided anything yet. Justices' questions are not rulings or votes. A decision will come later, and this explainer makes no prediction about it. [official source, official source]
